claim: 4-thio-uracil (4TU) is efficiently incorporated into nascent RNA.
source: We and others previously demonstrated that thio-modified uracil nucleobases, such as 4-thio-uracil (4TU) are efficiently incorporated into nascent RNA (Munchel et al., 2011; Miller et al., 2011; Cleary et al., 2005; Dölken et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior work

claim: Metabolic labeling with 4TU at appropriate concentrations has no adverse effect on cell proliferation.
source: Metabolic labeling with 4TU at appropriate concentrations has no adverse effect on cell proliferation and does not lead to major changes in gene expression (Sun et al., 2012; Miller et al., 2011) (see Appendix 1).
evidence: Supported by citations and reference to appendix

claim: Metabolic labeling with 4TU does not lead to major changes in gene expression.
source: Metabolic labeling with 4TU at appropriate concentrations has no adverse effect on cell proliferation and does not lead to major changes in gene expression (Sun et al., 2012; Miller et al., 2011) (see Appendix 1).
evidence: Supported by citations and reference to appendix

claim: The average mRNA half-life in rapidly dividing budding yeast is 4.8 minutes.
source: The new measurements with our improved protocol revealed a much less stable transcriptome than previously reported, with average and median mRNA half-lives of 4.8 and 3.6 min respectively (Figure 1C).
evidence: Measured experimentally using improved metabolic labeling protocol

claim: The median mRNA half-life in rapidly dividing budding yeast is 3.6 minutes.
source: The new measurements with our improved protocol revealed a much less stable transcriptome than previously reported, with average and median mRNA half-lives of 4.8 and 3.6 min respectively (Figure 1C).
evidence: Measured experimentally using improved metabolic labeling protocol

claim: The half-life of the bulk transcriptome in yeast is 13.1 minutes.
source: By summing the abundance of all mRNAs, we calculated the half-life of the bulk transcriptome to be 13.1 min (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).

claim: The bulk polyA(+) RNA pool half-life measured by 4TU chase (13.1 min) agrees well with 14C-adenine pulse labeling data (11.5 min).
source: Our measurement using thio-uracil chase agrees remarkably well with 14C-adenine pulse labeling data which reported a 11.5 min half-life for the bulk polyA(+) RNA pool in the cell (Petersen et al., 1976).

claim: Long-lived transcripts are functionally enriched for translation factors.
source: Consistent with the extensive protocol optimization, we found an overall poor correlation with our previously published dataset (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F). Nonetheless, our current measurements are consistent with the findings of Munchel et al. that long-lived (>1 SD above the mean) transcripts are functionally enriched for translation factors and that ribosomal protein-encoding mRNAs specifically are long lived as a group with an average half-life of 15.5 min (Figure 1—figure supplement 1.G; Figure 1—figure supplement 1.H) (Munchel et al., 2011).
evidence: Functional enrichment analysis of experimental data

claim: Ribosomal protein-encoding mRNAs are long lived as a group with an average half-life of 15.5 minutes.
source: Nonetheless, our current measurements are consistent with the findings of Munchel et al. that long-lived (>1 SD above the mean) transcripts are functionally enriched for translation factors and that ribosomal protein-encoding mRNAs specifically are long lived as a group with an average half-life of 15.5 min (Figure 1—figure supplement 1.G; Figure 1—figure supplement 1.H) (Munchel et al., 2011).

claim: Global inhibition of transcription induces a general stress response.
source: This stress response is elicited regardless of the method of global transcription inhibition be it by pharmacological or genetic means.

claim: Methods using transcriptional inhibition have off-target effects on cell physiology.
source: The second complication arises from the fact that the methods used to shutoff transcription have off-target effects themselves. Temperature shock or the use of transcriptional inhibitors such as phenantroline and thiolutin have unintended effects on cell physiology independent of transcriptional inhibition (Sun et al., 2012; Harigaya and Parker, 2016).

claim: Key factors in the decay pathway (Pat1, Dhh1, Ccr4, Xrn1) are regulated in a carbon source-dependent manner.
source: However, shutoff of the GAL promoter requires an acute carbon source shift and it has been shown that several key factors in the decay pathway such as Pat1, Dhh1, Ccr4 and Xrn1 are regulated in a carbon source-dependent manner (Ramachandran et al., 2011; Braun et al., 2014).

claim: mRNA half-life positively correlates with transcript abundance.
source: Our decay data clustered with transcript abundance, metrics of codon usage (normalized translational efficiency (nTE) and codon adaptation index (CAI)), as well as translational efficiency measured by ribosome footprinting (Pechmann and Frydman, 2013; Drummond et al., 2006).

claim: mRNA half-life positively correlates with codon usage metrics (nTE and CAI).
source: Our decay data clustered with transcript abundance, metrics of codon usage (normalized translational efficiency (nTE) and codon adaptation index (CAI)), as well as translational efficiency measured by ribosome footprinting (Pechmann and Frydman, 2013; Drummond et al., 2006).

claim: mRNA half-life positively correlates with translational efficiency measured by ribosome footprinting.
source: Our decay data clustered with transcript abundance, metrics of codon usage (normalized translational efficiency (nTE) and codon adaptation index (CAI)), as well as translational efficiency measured by ribosome footprinting (Pechmann and Frydman, 2013; Drummond et al., 2006).

claim: mRNA half-life negatively correlates with polyA-tail length.
source: Interestingly, mRNA half-life was negatively correlated with polyA-tail length consistent with prior observations (see discussion) (Subtelny et al., 2014).

claim: Bulk mRNA degradation is initiated by the removal of the polyA tail.
source: Bulk mRNA degradation was shown to be initiated by the removal of the polyA tail (Shyu et al., 1991; Muhlrad and Parker, 1992).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work

claim: After deadenylation, mRNAs can be degraded from the 3' end by the exosome complex.
source: This triggers degradation through one of two pathways. mRNAs can either be degraded from the 3' end by the exosome complex of 3' to 5' exonucleases or -what is thought to be more common in yeast- deadenylation is followed by removal of the 5'-methylguanosine cap by the decapping complex (Muhlrad et al., 1994; Decker and Parker, 1993).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work

claim: In yeast, deadenylation is more commonly followed by removal of the 5'-methylguanosine cap by the decapping complex.
source: mRNAs can either be degraded from the 3' end by the exosome complex of 3' to 5' exonucleases or -what is thought to be more common in yeast- deadenylation is followed by removal of the 5'-methylguanosine cap by the decapping complex (Muhlrad et al., 1994; Decker and Parker, 1993).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work

claim: After cap removal, mRNA is digested from the 5' end by the cytoplasmic 5' to 3' exonuclease Xrn1.
source: Removal of the cap structure is then followed by exonucleolytic digestion from the 5' end of the mRNA by the cytoplasmic 5' to 3' exonuclease, Xrn1.
evidence: Established knowledge about mRNA decay pathway

claim: Treatment with low dose cycloheximide (0.2 μg/mL) stabilizes CIS3 and RPL25 transcripts.
source: Even with this low concentration of cycloheximide, the CIS3 and RPL25 transcripts remained stabilized and the ACT1 mRNA again was not significantly affected (Figure 3B).

claim: Treatment with low dose cycloheximide (0.2 μg/mL) does not significantly affect ACT1 mRNA stability.
source: Even with this low concentration of cycloheximide, the CIS3 and RPL25 transcripts remained stabilized and the ACT1 mRNA again was not significantly affected (Figure 3B).

claim: The effects of cycloheximide on mRNA turnover are specific to elongation inhibition.
source: The effects of cycloheximide on mRNA turnover were specific to elongation inhibition as mRNA half-lives were unchanged in a cycloheximide resistant mutant (rpl28-Q38K) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).

claim: Treatment with sordarin stabilizes mRNA half-lives.
source: When cells were treated with a sub-lethal dose of sordarin, we again observed a stabilizing effect on mRNA half-lives (Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).

claim: Sordarin blocks the function of eukaryotic elongation factor 2.
source: We next tested an alternative translation elongation inhibitor, sordarin, which blocks the function of eukaryotic elongation factor 2 (Shastry et al., 2001).

claim: mRNA synthesis rates are not reduced upon treatment with cycloheximide or sordarin.
source: These stabilization effects were not due to an inability to incorporate 4TU into newly made transcripts as mRNA synthesis rates were not reduced upon treatment with either cycloheximide or sordarin (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D and E).

claim: Treatment with 3AT (5 mM) in gcn2∆ cells stabilizes 11 out of 15 examined mRNAs.
source: We examined the stability of 15 mRNAs with diverse spacing and position of histidine codons either untreated or treated with 3AT. Of these 15 paired measurements, we found that 11 are significantly stabilized and support the translation factor protection model (p(TP)<0.05).

claim: 3AT stalls ribosomes at histidine codons.
source: Indeed 3AT has previously been shown to stall ribosomes at histidine codons (Guydosh and Green, 2014).

claim: 3AT causes histidine starvation by lowering the concentration of histidyl-tRNAs.
source: To best mimic a non-optimal codon where the acceptor-site would be unoccupied, we treated cells with a sub-lethal dose (5 mM) of 3-amino-1,2,4-triazole (3AT), which results in histidine starvation thus lowering the concentration of histidyl-tRNAs (Figure 3—figure supplement 1F) (Klopotowski and Wiater, 1965).
evidence: Supported by citation and experimental observation

claim: 3AT treatment induces global mRNA stabilization across the transcriptome.
source: The stabilizing effects of 3AT that we observed at the single transcript level were also seen in a highly significant manner across the transcriptome (two-sided Wilcoxian paired test: p=1.165e-199) (Figure 3H).

claim: Inhibiting translation elongation by three different methods leads to overall stabilization of mRNAs.
source: Altogether, we conclude that inhibiting translation elongation by three different methods led to an overall stabilization of mRNAs.
evidence: Summary of experimental results from multiple approaches

claim: The observations from elongation inhibition experiments support a translation factor-protection model.
source: These observations are not consistent with the predictions of the stalled ribosome-triggered decay model but instead support a translation factor-protection model.

claim: Treatment with hippuristanol destabilizes ACT1, CIS3, and RPL25 mRNAs.
source: We observed that ACT1, CIS3 and RPL25 mRNAs all decayed with faster kinetics when eIF4A was inhibited (Figure 3I).

claim: Hippuristanol is an inhibitor of eukaryotic initiation factor 4A (eIF4A).
source: We first made use of hippuristanol, an inhibitor of eukaryotic initiation factor 4A (eIF4A) (Bordeleau et al., 2006).

claim: Simultaneous downregulation of eIF4E and eIF4G function destabilizes ACT1 and CIS3 transcripts.
source: As with hippuristanol-treated cells, we found that ACT1 and CIS3 transcripts were significantly destabilized while the RPL25 transcript was not significantly affected when translation initiation is slowed (Figure 3J).

claim: Cycloheximide induces global stabilization of mRNAs across the transcriptome.
source: In support of our observations with individual mRNAs, cycloheximide induced a global stabilization of mRNAs (p=6.298e-106 two-sided Wilcoxon paired test) whereas hippuristanol treatment led to shorter mRNA half-lives (p=1.864e-260 two-sided Wilcoxon paired test) (Figure 3K).

claim: Hippuristanol treatment leads to shorter mRNA half-lives across the transcriptome.
source: In support of our observations with individual mRNAs, cycloheximide induced a global stabilization of mRNAs (p=6.298e-106 two-sided Wilcoxon paired test) whereas hippuristanol treatment led to shorter mRNA half-lives (p=1.864e-260 two-sided Wilcoxon paired test) (Figure 3K).

claim: The efficiency of translation initiation is a major determinant of transcript stability on a transcriptome-wide level.
source: We conclude that slowing initiation accelerates mRNA turnover while inhibiting elongation slows mRNA turnover and that on a transcriptome-wide level, the efficiency of initiation either directly through 5'-cap competition or indirectly through ribosome protection is a major determinant of transcript stability.

claim: Inhibition of elongation with cycloheximide inhibits the formation of processing bodies.
source: Inhibition of elongation with cycloheximide was previously shown to inhibit the formation of processing bodies (PBs), which are thought to be sites of transcript repression and decay (Sheth and Parker, 2003; Kroschwald et al., 2015; Mugler et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work

claim: Hippuristanol induces processing body formation in a concentration dependent manner.
source: Interestingly, hippuristanol induced PB formation in a concentration dependent manner: at high doses (10–40 μM), rapid and robust PB formation could be observed; at an intermediate dose (5 μM), PBs formed over time and at a low dose (2.5 μM), PBs could not be detected (Figure 4A and B).

claim: GFA1, PGK1, and FBA1 mRNAs rapidly relocalize to processing bodies upon hippuristanol-induced PB formation.
source: Consistent with such a model, we observed the rapid relocalization of three distinct mRNAs, GFA1, PGK1 and FBA1, to PBs upon hippuristanol-induced PB formation (Figure 4D).

claim: Hippuristanol does not trigger the formation of stress granules in yeast.
source: Unlike in mammalian cell culture systems, hippuristanol does not trigger the formation of stress granules in yeast (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A) but as with other PBs, the formation of hippuristanol-induced Dhh1- and Dcp2-containing foci requires the RNA and ATP binding activities of Dhh1 as mutants of Dhh1 that are unable to bind RNA (dhh13x-RNA) or ATP (dhh1Q-motif) do not form PBs upon hippuristanol treatment (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B–C) (Mugler et al., 2016; Mazroui et al., 2006).

claim: Formation of hippuristanol-induced PBs requires the RNA and ATP binding activities of Dhh1.
source: Unlike in mammalian cell culture systems, hippuristanol does not trigger the formation of stress granules in yeast (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A) but as with other PBs, the formation of hippuristanol-induced Dhh1- and Dcp2-containing foci requires the RNA and ATP binding activities of Dhh1 as mutants of Dhh1 that are unable to bind RNA (dhh13x-RNA) or ATP (dhh1Q-motif) do not form PBs upon hippuristanol treatment (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B–C) (Mugler et al., 2016; Mazroui et al., 2006).

claim: Co-treatment of hippuristanol with cycloheximide or sordarin suppresses processing body formation.
source: However, co-treatment of hippuristanol-treated cells with either cycloheximide or sordarin suppressed PB formation, suggesting that the increased number of ribosome-unbound mRNA clients available for degradation, rather than crippled translation, was causative for PB formation (Figure 4A and C).

claim: A PP7sl-containing transcript rapidly localizes to processing bodies upon hippuristanol addition.
source: As observed for endogenous mRNAs, we found that the PP7sl-containing transcript rapidly localized to PBs (Figure 4E).

claim: The PP7-mRNA signal decays over time within processing bodies.
source: Moreover, we found that the PP7-mRNA signal decayed over time within the PB (Figure 4E and F).

claim: mRNAs can be degraded after they localize to processing bodies.
source: This suggests that mRNAs localize to PBs when initiation is inhibited and that these mRNAs can be degraded after they localize to a PB.

claim: Inhibiting translation initiation leads to global mRNA destabilization which causes the formation of processing bodies.
source: In combination with our metabolic labeling studies, we further conclude that inhibiting translation initiation leads to global mRNA destabilization which in turn causes the formation of PBs.

claim: Translation initiation is the central hub in globally regulating mRNA stability.
source: Taken together, these approaches have enabled us to identify translation initiation as the central hub in globally regulating mRNA stability.

claim: Estimated translation initiation rates strongly correlate with transcript half-life.
source: While no direct measurement of translation initiation rates at the transcriptome-wide level has been reported, rates estimated by using a kinetic model of ribosome flux (Ciandrini et al., 2013) are in agreement with our conclusion and the dataset of estimated rates strongly correlates and clusters most closely with transcript half-life (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–B).

claim: The overall stabilities of the transcriptome are similar with or without polyA selection.
source: We also profiled the stability of the transcriptome in the absence of polyA selection by sequencing unselected, total RNAs after metabolic labeling. We found that the overall stabilities were similar: in the absence of polyA selection, the average and median mRNA half-lives were 4.9 and 4.0 min respectively compared to 4.8 and 3.6 min with polyA selection (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).

claim: For the majority of transcripts, deadenylation is the rate determining step for decay.
source: Nevertheless, we conclude that the overall stability of the transcriptome remains largely unchanged in the absence of polyA selection indicating that for the majority of transcripts, deadenylation is the rate determining step for decay.

claim: 92% of transcripts are labeled and separated with >90% efficiency.
source: The analysis of the efficiency parameter showed that 92% of transcripts are labeled and separated with >90% efficiency and 98% of transcripts are labeled and separated with >80% efficiency indicating that our experimental optimizations are performing well (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Analysis of efficiency parameter from experimental data

claim: 84% of transcripts fit the modified exponential decay model with an R2 of >0.95.
source: Moreover, our data displayed a good fit to our modified exponential decay model with 84% of transcripts fitting with an R2 of >0.95 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).

claim: Half-lives were measured for 5378 of the 6464 annotated transcripts in rapidly dividing budding yeast.
source: Using this protocol, we measured half-life values for 5378 of the 6464 annotated transcripts in rapidly dividing budding yeast with a high agreement between biological replicates (Pearson correlation = 0.90) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).

claim: Biological replicates of half-life measurements show high agreement (Pearson correlation = 0.90).
source: Using this protocol, we measured half-life values for 5378 of the 6464 annotated transcripts in rapidly dividing budding yeast with a high agreement between biological replicates (Pearson correlation = 0.90) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).

claim: The yeast transcriptome is much more dynamic than previously measured, with an average transcript half-life of only 4.8 minutes.
source: Our refined measurements also reveal a remarkably dynamic transcriptome with an average mRNA half-life of only 4.8 min - much shorter than previously thought.
evidence: Experimental measurement compared to prior studies

claim: Global mRNA destabilization by inhibition of translation initiation induces dose-dependent formation of processing bodies.
source: Furthermore, global mRNA destabilization by inhibition of translation initiation induces a dose-dependent formation of processing bodies in which mRNAs can decay over time.

claim: mRNAs can decay over time in processing bodies.
source: Furthermore, global mRNA destabilization by inhibition of translation initiation induces a dose-dependent formation of processing bodies in which mRNAs can decay over time.

claim: mRNA degradation is tightly coupled to the regulation of translation.
source: Here, we combine non-invasive transcriptome-wide mRNA production and stability measurements with selective and acute perturbations to demonstrate that mRNA degradation is tightly coupled to the regulation of translation, and that a competition between translation initiation and mRNA decay -but not codon optimality or elongation- is the major determinant of mRNA stability in yeast.

claim: A competition between translation initiation and mRNA decay is the major determinant of mRNA stability in yeast.
source: Here, we combine non-invasive transcriptome-wide mRNA production and stability measurements with selective and acute perturbations to demonstrate that mRNA degradation is tightly coupled to the regulation of translation, and that a competition between translation initiation and mRNA decay -but not codon optimality or elongation- is the major determinant of mRNA stability in yeast.

claim: Codon optimality is not the major determinant of mRNA stability in yeast.
source: Here, we combine non-invasive transcriptome-wide mRNA production and stability measurements with selective and acute perturbations to demonstrate that mRNA degradation is tightly coupled to the regulation of translation, and that a competition between translation initiation and mRNA decay -but not codon optimality or elongation- is the major determinant of mRNA stability in yeast.

claim: Translation elongation is not the major determinant of mRNA stability in yeast.
source: Here, we combine non-invasive transcriptome-wide mRNA production and stability measurements with selective and acute perturbations to demonstrate that mRNA degradation is tightly coupled to the regulation of translation, and that a competition between translation initiation and mRNA decay -but not codon optimality or elongation- is the major determinant of mRNA stability in yeast.

claim: With an estimated average translation initiation rate of 0.12 s−1, the average transcript can code for about 50 polypeptides before it is destroyed.
source: Despite these very short half-lives, with an estimated average translation initiation rate of 0.12 s−1, this implies that the average transcript can still code for about 50 polypeptides before it is destroyed (Ciandrini et al., 2013).
evidence: Calculation based on measured half-lives and estimated initiation rates

claim: The overall instability of the transcriptome argues against the need for regulated mRNA decay for the bulk of transcripts in the cell.
source: This overall instability of the transcriptome argues against the need for regulated mRNA decay for the bulk of transcripts in the cell.

claim: Processing bodies are thought to be sites of transcript repression and decay.
source: Inhibition of elongation with cycloheximide was previously shown to inhibit the formation of processing bodies (PBs), which are thought to be sites of transcript repression and decay (Sheth and Parker, 2003; Kroschwald et al., 2015; Mugler et al., 2016).

claim: Processing body formation is directly dependent on the number of mRNA substrates available for degradation.
source: Our results show that hippuristanol generates client mRNAs for the decay machinery through its inhibition of initiation. The observed dosage effect therefore suggests that PB formation is directly dependent on the number of mRNA substrates available for degradation and that microscopic PBs can only be detected when a certain threshold of decay targets is reached.

claim: Microscopic processing bodies can only be detected when a certain threshold of decay targets is reached.
source: The observed dosage effect therefore suggests that PB formation is directly dependent on the number of mRNA substrates available for degradation and that microscopic PBs can only be detected when a certain threshold of decay targets is reached.

claim: mRNAs can decay co-translationally.
source: Yet, it has also been shown that mRNAs can decay co-translationally (Hu et al., 2009).

claim: Most mRNAs are likely decayed in mRNPs that have exited translation and are composed of deadenylation, decapping and exo-nucleolytic factors existing apart from microscopically visible processing bodies.
source: We therefore favor a model in which most mRNAs are decayed in mRNPs that have exited translation and are composed of deadenylation, decapping and exo-nucleolytic factors existing apart from microscopically visible PBs (Teixeira and Parker, 2007).
evidence: Inference from experimental observations and prior work

claim: The measured average mRNA half-life of 4.8 minutes is three times faster than previously measured by metabolic labeling.
source: A revelation from this work is the overall short half-life of the transcriptome, only 4.8 min or a mean lifetime of 6.9 min. This value is three times faster than was previously measured by metabolic labeling and up to 26 times faster than what was measured by transcriptional inhibition.

claim: The measured average mRNA half-life of 4.8 minutes is up to 26 times faster than what was measured by transcriptional inhibition.
source: A revelation from this work is the overall short half-life of the transcriptome, only 4.8 min or a mean lifetime of 6.9 min. This value is three times faster than was previously measured by metabolic labeling and up to 26 times faster than what was measured by transcriptional inhibition.

claim: The mean lifetime of the yeast transcriptome is 6.9 minutes.
source: A revelation from this work is the overall short half-life of the transcriptome, only 4.8 min or a mean lifetime of 6.9 min.
